reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: The hallmark is an intensely itchy, serpiginous (snake-like), slightly raised erythematous track that advances a short distance each day
It commonly affects the feet, buttocks, and other skin that contacts contaminated sand or soil, reflecting exposure during beach holidays or barefoot activity in warm climates
Take a travel and exposure history, as most cases in temperate regions are imported from tropical and subtropical areas
The larva itself lies just ahead of the visible track, so the leading edge marks its current position
It is a self-limiting zoonotic infestation because the human is a dead-end host in which the animal hookworm larva cannot complete its life cycle
Antihelminthic therapy shortens symptoms and is warranted for troublesome disease; the itch responds as the larva dies and the track resolves
Secondary bacterial infection from scratching and, less often, a localised allergic reaction can complicate the picture
Preventive advice includes wearing footwear and using barriers on contaminated sand or soil
reference.pathophysiology: Cutaneous larva migrans is caused by the larvae of animal hookworms, most often Ancylostoma species from dogs and cats, whose eggs are shed in animal faeces and hatch into infective larvae in warm, moist sand or soil. On contact these larvae penetrate intact human skin but lack the enzymes to cross the basement membrane, so they remain trapped in the epidermis. As the larva migrates it provokes a local eosinophilic inflammatory and hypersensitivity response that produces the itchy, advancing serpiginous track. Because humans are accidental dead-end hosts, the parasite cannot mature or disseminate and eventually dies, giving the self-limiting course.
additionalDifferentials: Larva currens due to Strongyloides (faster-moving track, often perianal)
Loiasis or other migratory parasitic eruptions in the appropriate exposure setting
additionalInvestigations: Diagnosis is clinical, based on the characteristic migrating track and exposure history
Dermoscopy may help visualise the larval track
Blood eosinophilia is variable and non-specific
Biopsy is usually unhelpful because the larva lies ahead of the visible track and is rarely captured
Assessment for secondary bacterial infection when the site is inflamed or purulent
redFlags: Extensive involvement or numerous tracks suggesting heavy exposure or an immunocompromised host
Rapidly moving perianal tracks or features suggesting Strongyloides, which can disseminate and requires different management
Signs of secondary bacterial infection such as spreading erythema, pain, or pus
Systemic symptoms or respiratory features prompting reconsideration of a diagnosis with visceral involvement
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and self-limiting, as the larva dies within weeks to a few months even without treatment; antihelminthic therapy shortens the intensely itchy course and speeds resolution, and lasting sequelae are uncommon apart from transient post-inflammatory change.
pitfalls: Failing to elicit a travel or sand-exposure history and missing the diagnosis
Confusing it with the faster-moving larva currens of Strongyloides, which carries a risk of dissemination
Performing an unhelpful biopsy at the visible track rather than treating clinically
Overlooking secondary bacterial infection driven by scratching
